name: Moral Realism
statement: There are objective moral facts: some moral claims are simply true, independent of what anyone thinks.
statementAccent: some moral claims are simply true
meaning: Moral realism is the metaethical view that there are objective moral facts or truths, so that moral claims, such as that torturing innocents for fun is wrong, can be objectively true or false, and at least some of them are true, independently of what any person or culture thinks or feels. Moral realism combines three commitments: cognitivism, the view that moral statements express beliefs and are apt to be true or false; the claim that at least some such statements are literally true; and the claim that their truth is objective or stance-independent, holding apart from human attitudes and desires. Moral realism contrasts with several anti-realist positions. Non-cognitivism, or expressivism, holds that moral statements do not report facts at all but express attitudes or emotions and so are not truth-apt, as in emotivism and prescriptivism. The error theory of J. L. Mackie holds that moral statements do purport to report facts and are truth-apt but are all systematically false, because there are no moral facts. And moral relativism and subjectivism hold that moral truth is relative to individuals or cultures rather than objective. Moral realism itself divides into naturalist versions, which take moral facts to be natural facts, and non-naturalist versions, which take them to be sui generis, as in G. E. Moore. It is a central and much-debated position in metaethics.
mechanism: Moral realism makes a set of connected claims about the status of moral judgments. First, it holds that when people make moral claims, they are expressing beliefs, cognitive states that represent the world as being a certain way, and that these claims are the kind of thing that can be true or false, a thesis called cognitivism. Second, it holds that at least some moral claims are in fact true, so that moral discourse succeeds in stating truths and is not uniformly mistaken. Third, and most distinctively, it holds that the truth of these moral claims is objective, or stance-independent: a claim like that gratuitous cruelty is wrong is true because of how things are morally, not because of what any individual or society happens to believe, desire, or approve. Moral realists divide over the nature of moral facts. Naturalist realists, such as those in the Cornell realist tradition, hold that moral facts are natural facts, in principle discoverable by empirical inquiry, for instance facts about well-being. Non-naturalist realists, such as Moore, hold that moral facts and properties are sui generis, of their own irreducible kind, not identical to any natural property, and known by a special kind of insight. Realists support their view by appeal to the way moral discourse presupposes objectivity, the possibility of moral progress and error, and the convergence of moral opinion, while defending against anti-realist objections.

examples.text: For a moral realist, that torturing innocents for fun is wrong is objectively true, independent of anyone's opinion.
Naturalist realists take moral facts to be natural facts, while non-naturalists like Moore take them to be sui generis.
Moral realism opposes Mackie's error theory, which agrees moral claims are truth-apt but holds they are all false.

variants.name: Naturalist versus non-naturalist realism
variants.text: Moral facts as natural facts discoverable by inquiry, versus moral facts as sui generis and irreducible.

variants.name: The anti-realist rivals
variants.text: Non-cognitivism, error theory, and relativism, which deny objective moral facts in different ways.

whyItMatters: Moral realism is one of the central positions in metaethics, the branch of philosophy concerned with the status and foundations of morality, and the question of whether it is true bears on how we understand the whole enterprise of ethics. If moral realism is correct, then moral claims can be objectively true, moral disagreement can be genuine disagreement about facts, and moral progress and moral error are real possibilities, so that ethics is a domain of knowledge to be discovered rather than a matter of taste or convention. If it is false, then the objectivity that ordinary moral discourse seems to presuppose is an illusion, and morality must be understood in some other way, as the expression of attitudes, a systematic error, or a matter relative to cultures. The debate between moral realism and its rivals, non-cognitivism, error theory, and relativism, is thus foundational to ethics and shapes how we interpret moral language, moral motivation, and moral disagreement. It also connects to deep questions about the place of value in a natural world.

working.text: hold that moral statements express beliefs that can be true or false, the cognitivist commitment.
maintain that at least some moral claims are actually true, not all mistaken.
hold that their truth is stance-independent, obtaining apart from anyone's attitudes or desires.

limits: Moral realism is a major position but faces influential objections, especially from J. L. Mackie. His argument from queerness holds that objective moral facts and properties would be metaphysically and epistemologically strange, entities or relations utterly unlike anything else in the universe and requiring a special faculty to know, so their existence should be doubted. His argument from relativity, or disagreement, holds that the wide and persistent variation of moral views across cultures is better explained by their reflecting different ways of life than by objective moral facts to which people have unequal access. Realists reply that disagreement does not by itself disprove objective facts and that many moral disagreements trace to differing factual beliefs over shared values, but the objections remain live. Realism also divides internally between naturalist and non-naturalist versions facing different problems, such as the open question argument against naturalism.
misreadings: Moral realism is not the claim that morality is obvious or that everyone agrees; it holds that some moral claims are objectively true, which is compatible with widespread disagreement and error. It is not the same as thinking morality comes from God or from a particular culture, since realists locate moral truth in stance-independent facts, whether natural or sui generis. And it is not established beyond doubt, since Mackie's arguments from queerness and disagreement are serious challenges, so treating moral realism as requiring consensus, as tied to one source like religion, or as uncontested, misreads a central but debated metaethical view.
origin: The metaethical view that there are objective, stance-independent moral facts and that some moral claims are true, contrasted with non-cognitivism, error theory, and relativism, and dividing into naturalist and non-naturalist versions.
